placebo.note: Identical prompt and identical pipeline for both arms; only the news differs. The clean stratum is the pre-declared primary comparison.

blind_match.caveat: The all-sections arm is inflated by generic world news: in the ceiling test, non-business sections matched at 90% while business-only matched at 16.7% against 8.3% chance (p=0.27). The business arm also has far less text (median 183 words vs 2772), so that gap is partly power and not only content. Both arms are reported; neither alone is the answer.

claims.claim: Iran, the US, UK, France, Russia, China, Germany and the EU reached a breakthrough framework agreement on Iran's nuclear programme, without signing an official document, with a deadline set for a full deal.
Saudi-led air strikes on Yemen intensified during the window, with heavy strikes in the south killing at least 20 Houthi fighters and Saudi Arabia claiming 500 rebels killed since operations began.
The WHO estimated roughly 560 dead, more than 1,700 injured and over 100,000 displaced after three weeks of intensified fighting.
A no-fly zone was declared over Yemen and India evacuated 5,600 people including 960 foreign nationals.

Russia convened a UN Security Council session on Saudi strikes in Yemen after a refugee camp was bombed, and Pakistan's parliament voted not to join the Saudi-led coalition, indicating diplomatic friction around the campaign.
Saudi Arabia also air-dropped weapons and medical supplies into the conflict zone.

A Japanese court in Fukui Prefecture issued a landmark injunction blocking the restart of two reactors at the Takahama Nuclear Power Plant, a decision bearing on utility operations and fuel-import demand.
On the flagged day the US president endorsed removing Cuba from the state sponsors of terrorism list, following a first leaders' meeting since the Cuban Revolution earlier in the window.
An Italian bank disclosed that its exposure to a single counterparty exceeded the regulatory limit, the only idiosyncratic financial-sector item in the window.
Eurozone finance ministers rejected a Greek request to extend debt negotiations beyond a Tuesday deadline.
The Hellenic Parliament approved holding a referendum on a proposed bailout, scheduled for the following Sunday.
Greek banks were experiencing steady deposit withdrawals, with over 3 billion euros pulled out, prompting the ECB to raise the cap on emergency liquidity assistance.
A senior Greek parliamentary figure had earlier warned that parliament might reject the concessions the government offered creditors, signalling political fragility ahead of the deadline.
The Governor of Puerto Rico stated that the territory's debts are "not payable".
The People's Bank of China cut interest rates for a fourth successive time to help stabilise growth.
Suicide bombings hit Brussels, with a metro station and the airport targeted by two brothers of Belgian nationality and a third bomber, a fourth suspect remaining at large.
One of the Brussels bombers was identified as the suspected bomb-maker who supplied suicide vests for the earlier Paris attacks, and further arrests followed in the Schaerbeek district.
The attacks produced immediate European policy fallout, with Poland abandoning its pledge to shelter Syrian migrants under the EU relocation agreement.
Public disorder followed in Brussels, with police using water cannon against a far-right demonstration at a tribute site, and one charged suspect was released for lack of corroborating evidence.
A suicide bombing by a Pakistani Taliban faction killed at least 60 and injured 300 at a park in Lahore, prompting an announced paramilitary crackdown in Punjab.
Brazil's Supreme Court ruled that Lula should be stripped of his cabinet role so he could be investigated in connection with the Petrobras kickback scheme.

On Day 13 a second impeachment request was filed against President Rousseff, a minister resigned, and the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party was expected to vote on leaving the governing coalition, while the presidency said a new coalition would be announced within the week.

Additional geopolitical friction accumulated in the window: repeated North Korean missile launches, US and European notification to the UN that Iranian missile launches violated a Security Council resolution, Russian missile-defence deployments to disputed islands and new units near NATO, and US orders for diplomats' and military families to leave southern Turkey over terrorist threats.

Corporate events in the window included a raised counterbid for Starwood Hotels at $14 billion, reported Microsoft financing for a possible Yahoo bid, and an EU competition halt to the Halliburton-Baker Hughes review.
A poll showed the "Leave" camp 10 points ahead of "Remain" in a substantial swing, with less than two weeks remaining before Britain's referendum on EU membership.
A car bomb near Istanbul's main tourism district killed eleven and wounded 36, and drew condemnation from the UN Secretary-General.
Two gunmen killed at least four people in Tel Aviv, after which Israel suspended 83,000 Palestinian entry permits and temporarily banned Palestinian entry.

A mass shooting at a nightclub in Orlando killed at least 50 people and was described as the deadliest mass shooting and worst terror attack in the United States since 9/11; a claim of responsibility was attributed to ISIL.
On the final day, an attacker killed a police officer and took his family hostage near Paris, ending with the mother dead.
On the final day, Microsoft agreed to acquire LinkedIn for $26.2 billion.

On the final day, the US Supreme Court struck down a Puerto Rico law permitting restructuring of public utility debts over creditor objections, with a $2 billion agency payment due and a prior $370 million default already recorded.
Militants blew up an Eni-operated oil pipeline in the Niger Delta, and Nigeria reported recovering $9.1 billion in assets stolen from the oil sector.

Geopolitical friction was also elevated: Japan summoned China's ambassador over a naval incursion near the Senkaku Islands, and Russia warned of retaliatory measures over a US destroyer's Black Sea deployment.

The window's most geopolitically dramatic event, an attempted military coup in Turkey, occurred at the very start of the window (Day 1-2) and was followed by a crackdown and a three-month state of emergency, not at the end when the model flagged.

Corporate and business items in the window are idiosyncratic single-company events rather than macro shocks: a Herbalife FTC settlement, Unilever's $1bn purchase of Dollar Shave Club, Verizon's $4.83bn purchase of Yahoo!, and a Tesla factory opening.

Items dated Day 13 and Day 14 concern a US party convention, regional flooding in Assam and Nepal, a Syrian jihadist group rebranding away from Al-Qaeda, and North Korean rhetoric about US sanctions on its leader.

The terrorism and mass-casualty events in the window (Germany axe and mall attacks, Kabul bombings, Qamishli bombings, Mogadishu bombings, Baton Rouge and Florida shootings) are geographically dispersed and none is described as affecting financial infrastructure, commodity supply, or policy.
No item in the window reports a central bank decision, an interest rate or inflation release, a currency move, an index level, a credit event, or a commodity price shock.

Financial analysts interpreted remarks by the U.S. Treasury Secretary as an indication that the United States may change the strong dollar policy held since the 1990s, noting the absence of the customary statement that a strong dollar is good for America.
The U.S. Senate confirmed a new chairman of the Federal Reserve during the window, by 84 votes to 13.
A U.S. government shutdown stalemate was live during the window, with the President publicly urging Senate Republicans to consider the 'nuclear option'.

At least one other market was recorded as moving during the window, with the Sao Paulo stock market hitting new highs and the Brazilian real strengthening amid political news about the presidential election.
The single item dated to the flag day itself is a hospital fire in South Korea with no described financial or economic consequences.

Geopolitical tension items in the window include a Turkish cross-border military campaign into northern Syria, rocket fire into a Turkish border city, and a UN Security Council emergency meeting request.
The window also includes an unresolved dispute over the Iran nuclear deal, with the U.S. President extending sanctions relief conditionally and Iran refusing any change to the deal.
The United States announced its withdrawal from the Iran nuclear deal on the day the model flagged.

Earlier in the window the leaders of the United Kingdom, Germany and France publicly agreed that the Iran nuclear deal was the best way to prevent Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons, indicating a transatlantic split over the agreement's future.
The regional security backdrop during the window included Israeli airstrikes on Hamas targets in Gaza and repeated shooting incidents at the Gaza fence.
Israel used a hotline to warn a Russian-operated airbase in Syria after a Russian jet approached Israeli airspace near the Golan Heights, following an earlier shoot-down of a Syrian warplane.
Saudi-led coalition airstrikes destroyed the presidential palace in Sana'a, Yemen, killing at least six.
Official results showed Hezbollah and allied parties winning a slight parliamentary majority.

Syrian government forces with what were believed to be Iranian-backed militias clashed with U.S.-backed Kurdish-led forces east of the Euphrates, with U.S.-led coalition jets involved in the counter-attack.

The single event dated to the flag day with any direct economic footprint is a Category 4 hurricane making landfall on the Florida Panhandle, which had been tracked as a strengthening storm over the preceding two days.
The window contains a first-round presidential election in Brazil, an event capable of moving emerging-market assets, three days before the flag day.

Corporate-specific news in the window includes an SEC settlement requiring Elon Musk and Tesla to pay $20 million each with Musk stepping down as chairman, a Facebook security flaw affecting 50 million accounts, and Google shutting its consumer Google+ product after a flaw potentially exposing 500,000 users' data.
Trade policy news in the window is de-escalatory rather than disruptive: Canada agreed to sign a replacement for the existing North American trade agreement.

The remaining items are natural disasters, criminal cases, national elections in Cameroon and Gabon, sports results, scientific prizes and discoveries, and diplomatic personnel news such as the resignation of the U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations.

Indian military aircraft crossed into Pakistani airspace and released a payload near Balakot, which India described as a strike on a militant camp in retaliation for an earlier attack; Pakistan scrambled its own jets in response.
The Hanoi summit between the US and North Korean leaders ended earlier than scheduled with the White House stating no deal had been reached on nuclear weapons or sanctions.
Attempts to move humanitarian aid into Venezuela led to trucks being set on fire, clashes with the National Guard and three deaths, followed by Venezuela severing diplomatic relations with Colombia.
The UN Security Council rejected rival US and Russian resolutions on Venezuela, with Russia and China vetoing the US text.

The UK Prime Minister told the Commons that if her deal and a no-deal exit were both rejected, MPs would be granted a vote on extending the departure deadline, and the opposition said it would back a second referendum absent support for its own plan.
The single item dated to the flag day is a US gubernatorial announcement of a presidential primary campaign, with no direct market relevance.

Company-level disruption in the window included a UK airline bankruptcy stranding passengers, a carmaker announcing closure of a UK plant with about 3,500 job losses, and another carmaker exiting commercial trucks in South America.
A threat by the U.S. president to raise tariffs on Chinese-made goods coincided with Chinese stocks falling more than 5% by midday and a sharp drop in U.S. stock futures.
The bilateral negotiations for a new trade deal, originally scheduled during the window, were reported to be in question after the tariff threat.
Separately, the United States deployed a carrier strike group and a bomber task force to the Middle East, with an official citing threats against U.S. maritime and land-based forces in the region.

Other conflict headlines in the window included Israeli airstrikes on Gaza in response to rocket fire, Syrian government forces taking territory in an ongoing offensive, and clashes involving Turkish forces in Iraq.
A single-name corporate credit item in the window reported that a bankrupt utility had failed to reach a settlement with creditors over billions of dollars owed under power purchase contracts.
Turkey's electoral authority annulled the Istanbul mayoral result and ordered a rerun, a domestic political shock in a major emerging market.
The United States announced 'major' sanctions on Iran early in the window, aimed at preventing nuclear weapons acquisition.

Saudi Arabia's minister of state for foreign affairs warned of a 'very, very strong reaction' if Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, and later called for 'action' on Iran while working with Japan and others on safe transit of the Persian Gulf.
On Day 13, Royal Marines seized an oil tanker off Gibraltar carrying Iranian crude bound for Syria; Iran called it an 'illegal seizure' and summoned the UK ambassador in Tehran.
Israel struck Iranian and Syrian military targets outside Damascus and Homs, killing 16, with a stray Syrian missile landing in Northern Cyprus.
A drone launched toward Saudi Arabia by Houthis was intercepted in Yemeni airspace.
At the G20 summit, Trump and Xi reached a deal permitting US sales of non-sensitive technology to Huawei in exchange for Chinese purchases of US food and agricultural products.
Hong Kong anti-extradition protesters briefly broke into the Legislative Council Complex.
AbbVie announced a plan to acquire Allergan for about $63 billion.
A magnitude 6.4 earthquake struck near Ridgecrest, Southern California, with no injuries reported.
On the final day of the window the U.S. Treasury Department issued a formal designation naming China (the specific label is not given in the item text).
On the same day, a Hong Kong city-wide general strike with sit-ins across seven districts cancelled over 200 flights, halted MTR lines, and coincided with a sharp fall in the Hang Seng Index.
Hong Kong's Chief Executive rejected protester demands and blamed them for 'destroying Hong Kong', indicating no near-term resolution.
The unrest in Hong Kong had been escalating through the window, including mass protests near China's Liaison Office in defiance of a police ban and an attack on pro-democracy activists.
Also on the final day, the UK announced it was joining a U.S.-led naval mission in the Persian Gulf to protect oil tankers after seizures by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
U.S.-Iran tension had already escalated earlier in the window with Treasury sanctions on Iran's foreign minister.
Separately, the U.S. was publicly weighing a blockade of Venezuela, another commodity-relevant escalation during the window.
Parliament passed an amendment requiring that no withdrawal agreement be approved until all relevant legislation is passed, obliging the Prime Minister to request an extension.
Parliament subsequently passed the Withdrawal Agreement Bill 329 to 299 but rejected its proposed timetable 322 to 308, leaving the bill described by the Speaker as 'in limbo'.
The European Commission announced agreement to a further extension of the deadline, with the length initially undecided, and the EU then agreed a specific delay date.
Argentine voters elected Alberto Fernández over incumbent Mauricio Macri, the first Argentine president to lose a re-election bid, by a narrower margin than polls predicted.

Chile declared a state of emergency covering roughly 52 percent of the population, the president said the country was 'at war', all sitting ministers were dismissed, and the government cancelled the APEC Summit and the UN Climate Change Conference it was due to host.

Bolivian authorities abruptly halted publication of election results with the incumbent at 45 percent and the challenger at 38 percent, prompting concern from the OAS, which later began an audit of the results.
The US House of Representatives voted 232 to 196 to formalise the procedures of the impeachment inquiry into the President.
Lebanon's prime minister resigned amid mass protests after the government had passed emergency economic measures.
A single large corporate/technology event occurred: a $10 billion government cloud computing contract was awarded to one major vendor over the expected winner.
Early in the window Chinese authorities reported a third coronavirus death, 136 new infections over a weekend, and confirmed spread from Wuhan to Shenzhen, Beijing and Hong Kong.
The entire city of Wuhan was quarantined, with all public transport suspended and no one permitted to leave, as the death toll reached 17.
North Korea banned foreign tourists and closed its border with China in response to the virus.
Commercial closures began, with Shanghai Disney Resort shutting temporarily ahead of the Lunar New Year.
China established a national leading group under Premier Li Keqiang and extended the Spring Festival holiday to contain the outbreak.
Hubei reported 1,291 new confirmed cases and 24 further deaths, taking the toll to 106.
China's president publicly addressed the World Health Organization about defeating the virus, indicating the outbreak had become an international health matter.

Containment actions spread beyond China: over 6,000 passengers were barred from disembarking a cruise ship in Italy over two suspected cases, and a repatriation flight carrying 195 Americans from China was quarantined on the flagged day.
The European Parliament voted 621-49 to pass the Brexit agreement, marking the last day Britain was represented in that parliament.

Numerous countries suspended use of the Oxford–AstraZeneca vaccine within a two-day span over reports of blood clots, including the Netherlands, Latvia, Cyprus, Slovenia, Andorra, Bulgaria, Italy's Piedmont region and others.
Germany resumed AstraZeneca vaccinations after the European Medicines Agency declared the vaccine safe, while France restricted it to those over 55.
Clinical trial results reported late in the window showed the AstraZeneca vaccine to be 79% effective.
Germany announced an 'emergency brake' and extended its nationwide lockdown, including shop closures, amid a spike in cases.

Other jurisdictions tightened restrictions during the window: Malta closed venues and schools, Bulgaria announced closures of theatres, cinemas, gyms and schools, Chile placed almost nine million people under quarantine, Metro Manila imposed a curfew, and Rajasthan imposed night curfews.
Record case or death counts were reported in Hungary, Ukraine, Turkey, the Philippines, India, Kenya and Mongolia during the window.
The US President signed a $1.9 trillion relief package into law on Day 2.
A Houthi drone strike caused a large fire at a Saudi Aramco oil refinery in Riyadh, with the group vowing continued operations against Saudi Arabia.

Geopolitical friction featured in the window: China's legislature rewrote Hong Kong's electoral rules, the UK declared China in breach of the Sino-British Joint Declaration, Russia recalled its ambassador to the US, and US and Chinese representatives met in Anchorage.
Overseas spectators were banned from the Tokyo Olympics and Paralympics due to COVID-19 risk.
The final day of the window contains no item of obvious market significance beyond routine vaccination news.
The US president warned Ukraine that Russia may invade, and Russia's foreign minister publicly denied interest in starting a war.
Belarus's president said his country might go to war if Belarus or Russia were attacked, while insisting Belarus does not want war with Ukraine.
Belarusian and Russian forces were shown conducting joint military drills in Belarus amid the tensions.
Belarus alleged a Ukrainian Air Force drone violated its airspace and summoned the Ukrainian ambassador.
Separatist authorities in Luhansk accused Ukraine of deploying an anti-aircraft system in a residential area near the frontline.
The window explicitly contains a topic entry for the Russo-Ukrainian crisis and Russia\u2013United States relations.
A US$66 billion semiconductor merger between Arm and Nvidia was cancelled under regulatory pressure, with Arm instead planning an IPO.
Items on the flagged day concern only COVID-19 infections of heads of state and royals, the lifting of Spain's outdoor mask mandate, and an archaeological discovery.

On the final day of the window, Russian forces launched at least 76 missiles across Ukraine, hitting at least nine power stations and killing at least three civilians, with Ukraine accusing Russia of weaponising winter.
The day before, Russian shelling killed two people and left the entire city of Kherson without power.
Fighting and attacks on infrastructure continued throughout the window, including shelling in Donetsk and the reported abduction of two senior staff from the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant.
The US Federal Trade Commission announced it would sue to block Microsoft's pending acquisition of Activision Blizzard on competition grounds.
Former FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried was arrested in the Bahamas at the request of the US government.
A US jury found the Trump Organization guilty of tax fraud charges.
Regional tensions also escalated, with Serbia requesting the return of security personnel to Kosovo and Kosovo formally applying for EU membership over Serbian objections.
The window contains no items describing central bank decisions, inflation data, or other scheduled macroeconomic releases.
China's Ministry of Finance announced 10–15% tariffs on a range of US food imports.
Canada announced a reciprocal 25% tariff on American goods worth up to US$155 billion.
Earlier in the window, the US president announced impending 25% tariffs on the European Union, to be applied broadly including to the automotive sector.

Consumer-level and retail-level backlash against US policy was already visible, with a Danish retail group controlling roughly a third of its national market moving to label European versus American brands, and a 24-hour consumer spending boycott in the United States.
Separately, the Gaza ceasefire's first phase ended with Israel blocking all humanitarian aid into Gaza and Hamas rejecting a US-led extension proposal.

Ukraine-related diplomacy was in flux: a US–Ukraine minerals deal was announced, the US State Department terminated support for Ukraine's energy grid restoration, and European leaders said they were preparing a peace plan to present to the US president.
Israel launched what it called a preemptive strike on Iran, killing senior officials including the supreme leader.
Iran, Iraq, Israel, Kuwait, Qatar and Syria closed their airspace to civilian flights and the UAE suspended flights from Dubai and Al Maktoum airports.

Iran struck targets across the Gulf, including airports in Abu Dhabi and Dubai, a hotel in Bahrain housing US embassy staff, the US embassies in Kuwait City and Riyadh, and the Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar.
Maersk suspended all vessel transits through the Strait of Hormuz until further notice.

Commercial shipping and energy infrastructure were hit: a tanker was struck by a missile in the Gulf of Oman, an oil terminal at Fujairah caught fire after a drone attack, a Bahraini oil refinery was hit, and an explosion damaged a tanker off Kuwait causing an oil spill.
UAE stock exchanges (Nasdaq Dubai, Dubai Financial Market, Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange) had been suspended for two days because of the Iranian strikes and were resuming on Day 13.
On the flagged day, South Korea's president activated a ₩100 trillion (about US$68 billion) stabilization fund explicitly to address financial market volatility linked to the Iran war.

Diplomatic de-escalation was not in prospect at the close of the window: Iran's security council secretary ruled out negotiations and the foreign minister said Iran was not seeking a ceasefire, despite Trump claiming talks had been agreed.

The conflict widened beyond the Gulf, with US forces sustaining six deaths, a US submarine sinking an Iranian warship off Sri Lanka, missiles fired toward Cyprus and a drone hitting RAF Akrotiri, and the UK deploying a warship to Cyprus.
Separately and earlier in the window, the US raised the global import tariff from 10% to 15% under emergency powers after a Supreme Court ruling against earlier country-specific tariffs.
Iran ileU.S. negotiations were an active, recurring news thread through the window.
Early in the window, gold rose to more than a one-week high on reports that Iran and the U.S. might be nearing a deal to end the war.
The U.S. president publicly rejected the Iranian response as "totally unacceptable", reversing the earlier optimistic tone.
Third parties (Pakistan, Turkey) were actively mediating, and near the end of the window Pakistan reportedly passed a revised Iranian proposal to the United States.
A drone strike targeted the Barakah nuclear power plant in the UAE, causing a fire, and the UAE said it intercepted three drones.

The UAE was reported to have secretly participated in strikes on Iran, including on an oil refinery on Lavan Island, and Israel was reported to have deployed air defences and personnel to the UAE amid Iranian strikes.

Strait of Hormuz transit was disrupted and contested: a Japanese shipper said three of its vessels crossed without paying transit fees, and a supertanker carrying 2 million barrels of Iraqi crude crossed after two months stranded in the Gulf.
The war was associated with a fuel crisis, and rising fuel prices partly attributed to the Iran war triggered deadly protests in the Comoros.

Iran-linked security incidents extended beyond the Gulf, including mass arrests in Bahrain and the arrest in Turkey of a Kata'ib Hezbollah commander accused of planning retaliatory attacks in the U.S. and Europe.
The U.S. Senate again blocked a War Powers Resolution seeking to curtail the president's war powers in the Iran war, by 49 ile50.
On the final day of the window the President of Russia announced a third peace agreement.

The announcement came after two weeks of active fighting and negotiation in eastern Ukraine, including peace talks held while fighting raged, a shell striking a hospital in rebel-held Donetsk that killed at least three, and an artillery shell causing a massive explosion at a Donetsk chemical plant.
Separately, gunmen stormed Libya's al-Mabrook oil field during the window, an event touching physical energy supply.

Corporate and market events in the window included Apple closing as the first company with a market capitalisation above $700 billion, Pfizer's $17 billion agreement to acquire Hospira, RadioShack's Chapter 11 filing, Siemens announcing 7,800 job cuts, and a CAN$1bn+ gold mining consolidation deal.
Other geopolitical stress in the window included the US, UK and France closing their Yemeni embassies and evacuating staff, and the confirmed death of an ISIL hostage.
Emerging-market capital flight was explicitly reported in one case, with foreign investors withdrawing billions of pesos from the Philippines after a deadly battle threatened a peace deal.

The only explicit market-index item in the window is a mid-window note that the Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed at record levels, which describes calm, rising markets rather than a shock.

Corporate news in the window is limited to a single large domestic merger announcement (Charter Communications and Time Warner Cable, $55.1 billion) and a report that Mediobanca intends to sell a 1.6% stake in Telecom Italia, neither of which is a systemic event.
The macroeconomic data point in the window is UK inflation turning negative at -0.1%, described as the first negative reading in many years.
A MERS outbreak in South Korea escalates across the window, from a third confirmed case to twelve cases by the final day.

Geopolitical items are numerous but locally contained: ISIS capture of Ramadi and displacement of tens of thousands, mosque bombings in Saudi Arabia, a bus attack in Balochistan, and calls by France and Germany for Russia to implement Minsk measures.

The most prominent institutional story of the window is the detention of six FIFA officials in Switzerland for extradition to the United States and the opening of Swiss criminal proceedings over World Cup awards, which has no direct financial-market channel.

The final day contains no financial or macroeconomic event of scale: a presidential inauguration in Nigeria, a volcanic eruption and evacuation in Japan, a surveillance-flight agreement, a car bomb, and a criminal sentencing.

The final day of the window contains a corporate reorganisation announcement in which Google creates a new holding company, Alphabet Inc., encompassing Google Inc. and other subsidiaries — a structural change at a single issuer rather than a macro shock.

The only genuine credit event in the window occurs a week before the flagged day: Puerto Rico misses a scheduled US$58 million payment against $72 billion of debt, and Moody's treats the commonwealth as in default.

Other economic and financial items are isolated and largely idiosyncratic: a Swiss National Bank first-half loss of CHF 50 billion attributed to an earlier peg removal, a central bank cut to 11% with the ruble down 1.5% to 60.60, an HSBC disposal of its Brazilian business for $5.2 billion, and a UK government sale of 5.4% of RBS raising £2.1bn.

The security events clustered on the flagged day — an attack on the US consulate in Istanbul claimed by DHKP-C, a suicide bombing at Kabul airport, and a fatal stabbing at a store in Sweden — caused few or no fatalities in the consulate case and involve no assets, infrastructure, or economies of systemic financial importance.

The remainder of the window is dominated by non-financial news: aircraft debris confirmed as belonging to a missing airliner, an escalating Turkey–PKK conflict, Boko Haram attacks and rescues in Nigeria, a typhoon threatening Taiwan, flooding in Myanmar, a legionnaires outbreak, and various crime and accident stories.

The only item in the window with a clear macro-financial transmission channel is the US Senate's failure to pass a resolution blocking the Iran nuclear agreement, meaning the deal will be formally adopted.

That outcome was already signalled more than a week earlier, when it was reported that the President had sufficient Senate support to sustain a veto, so the Day 13 confirmation carried little new information.

The remaining high-volume storylines are humanitarian and geopolitical rather than financial: a large-scale movement of refugees across Europe with national policy responses from Germany, Austria, Hungary, France, Denmark and Australia.

Business and economics items in the window are firm-specific and small in scale: a $765 million divestiture of a food brand, a limited vehicle recall, an Indian patent rejection for a single drug, and a German airline pilots' strike that was halted by court injunction.

Conflict items cluster around Turkey/PKK, Yemen, Syria and Iraq, including escalating Turkish air strikes on PKK targets on the flagged day, but none describes disruption to production, shipping or financial infrastructure.
Items dated to the flagged day itself are dominated by domestic legal, electoral and disaster news with no evident cross-market significance.
Iranian protesters ransacked and set fire to the Saudi Arabian embassy in Tehran in response to the Saudi execution of Nimr al-Nimr.
Saudi Arabia broke off diplomatic relations with Iran following the execution and the embassy attack.
On the final day of the window, Sudan, the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain also cut diplomatic relations with Iran.
Two Sunni mosques were bombed in central Iraq amid fears of renewed sectarian strife linked to the execution.
Separately, enriched uranium was shipped from Iran to Russia under an international agreement, with IAEA verification a precondition for dismantling economic sanctions on Iran.
Anti-terrorist operations continued at an Indian Air Force base in Pathankot, with six militants and seven military and paramilitary personnel reported killed.
Iraq's foreign minister demanded Turkish troop withdrawal from northern Iraq and raised the prospect of military action.
Denmark and Sweden introduced border identity checks despite all parties being Schengen signatories.
Saudi Arabia was reported to be sending troops and fighter jets to Turkey's Incirlik Air Base ahead of a planned ground invasion of Syria, with the deployment confirmed by Turkey's foreign minister.
Turkey's military shelled Kurdish PYD positions in northern Syria, including a recently captured airbase.
Turkey's prime minister accused Russia of acting as a 'terrorist organization' in Syria and threatened an 'extremely decisive response'.

At the Munich Security Conference, Russia's prime minister said tensions with NATO had pushed the world into a 'new Cold War', while NATO's secretary-general described relations as neither cold war nor partnership.
Kurdish-led forces took control of Tell Rifaat in Aleppo Governorate, continuing territorial change in the contested northern Syria area.
Ukraine and Russia imposed reciprocal bans on each other's cargo trucks transiting their territory.

Earlier in the window, North Korea conducted a long-range rocket launch condemned by the UN Security Council, with China backing a resolution to make it 'pay the necessary price', and North Korea froze South Korean assets at the Kaesong Industrial Park.
The only item dated to the flag day is the freeing of three Americans abducted in Baghdad by the Iraqi Intelligence Service.
Argentina's government made a $6.5 billion cash offer to holdout creditors to settle liabilities from a prior default.
Puerto Rico's governor announced the Commonwealth would default on a $422 million bond payment due the following Monday, suspending debt payments to fund essential services.
Congress had been unable to pass a debt restructuring bill for Puerto Rico, leaving no orderly legal mechanism for the default.
Donald Trump won the Indiana Republican primary on the final day of the window, following forecast wins in five state primaries a week earlier.
The Philippine peso became the worst performing currency in Asia as a result of a volatile and unpredictable presidential election.
The Philippine stock market suffered its biggest drop in months amid election uncertainty on the day before the flag.
Spain failed to form a government and a repeat parliamentary election was called, an unprecedented outcome for a country previously governed under a two-party system.
Hungary announced a referendum on future EU refugee resettlement quotas, and Finland's parliament debated a citizen petition on abandoning the euro amid a weakening economy.
The European Union opened an antitrust case accusing Google of abusing the dominance of Android by preloading its own apps.
UK retailer BHS, employing 11,000 people, collapsed into administration in the largest high street failure since Woolworths.
On Day 10 the UK voted to leave the EU and U.S. futures markets fell by 650 points.
The Dow Jones closed down 611.21 points to 17,399.86, its largest drop in ten months.
Standard & Poor's cut the UK credit rating from AAA to AA with a negative outlook, and Fitch cut it from AA+ to AA.
Analysts at Bank of America and Credit Suisse said the UK economy was heading into recession.
The EU refused informal talks with the UK until Article 50 is triggered, while Germany and France pressed for a rapid separation, leaving the process timetable contested.

Political fragmentation followed: a petition for a second referendum exceeded two million signatures, Scotland's First Minister sought talks with EU institutions about remaining, and Spain raised joint governance of Gibraltar.
The European Parliament's first debate on the vote on Day 14 was marked by bitter exchanges and heckling.
Before the vote, the European Commission president had warned there would be no re-negotiation with Britain whatever the referendum outcome.

The only item in the window with direct, large-scale financial-market relevance is the EU competition ruling ordering Apple to pay up to 13 billion euros ($14.5 billion) plus interest in back taxes to Ireland over 'illegal state aid'.
The single macroeconomic data point in the window was benign and positive: US new single-family home sales unexpectedly rose to their highest level in nearly nine years on broad-based demand.

The final day of the window contains only the announced signing date for the Colombia–FARC peace deal, a militant attack on Christians in Mardan, Pakistan, and the death of Uzbek President Islam Karimov after 27 years in office — none of which are described in market or economic terms.

The bulk of the window consists of terrorism, conflict and natural-disaster reporting — bombings in Turkey, Yemen, Somalia and Kyrgyzstan, an Italian earthquake with a death toll rising to at least 290, a 7.1 magnitude quake off New Zealand, and hurricane watches for Hawaii and Florida — geographically dispersed events with no stated linkage to financial markets.
Other economy-adjacent items are narrow or national in scope: a Philippine mining crackdown closing nickel and copper mines, and a Japanese plan to raise defence spending.

Politically notable but non-financial items include a Trump–Peña Nieto meeting in Mexico City, an investigation into hacking of US state election databases, and the killing of ISIL spokesman Abu Mohammad al-Adnani.
The UK Prime Minister announced a specific deadline for triggering Article 50 and plans for a 'Great Repeal Bill' to repeal the European Communities Act once the UK leaves the EU.
The pound reached a 31-year low against the US dollar following the Brexit vote.
Sterling sustained a flash crash, falling from about $1.23 to $1.13 within minutes before recovering much of the move, which observers attributed to algorithmic trading.
The FTSE 100 reached an all-time intraday high of 7,129, explicitly linked to the drop in the pound against the dollar.
At least one issuer publicly delayed an IPO citing concern over potential market volatility around the US presidential election.
On the final day of the window, the CEO and chairman of a major US bank resigned amid a scandal over sales practices.

Earlier in the window, a US settlement demand against a large European bank over toxic mortgage bonds was reported to have been lowered to about $5.4 billion from an initial demand of up to $14 billion.
On the day the model flagged, Bitcoin lost a third of its value within 24 hours.
Two days before the flag day, the US Senate and House passed the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, sending it to the President, and the law removes the individual insurance mandate from Obamacare.
On the flag day, pro-independence parties retained an absolute majority in a regional parliament and there was no clarity as to which party had the right to form a government.
Also on the flag day, Apple faced backlash and lawsuits after admitting it deliberately slowed some older phones, a company-specific legal overhang.
A European Court of Justice ruling reclassified Uber as a transport company subject to stricter EU regulation and licensing, a sector-level regulatory decision during the window.

Geopolitical background during the window included a Houthi missile fired at Riyadh and intercepted, US accusations that Iran violated the nuclear deal, and mass protests over US recognition of Jerusalem as Israel's capital.

The two items closest to the flagged day that touch on business and economy are the UK administrations of Maplin Electronics (2,500 jobs at risk) and Toys "R" Us UK (3,200 jobs at risk), both single-company retail failures rather than macro events.

The flagged day itself contains only political items: an Argentine presidential address opening congressional sessions, a Senate Intelligence Committee report on a leak of text messages, a generic entry on Russian interference in a US election, and an FBI-assisted Norwegian probe into forged Nobel nominations.

The most financially specific item in the window, the detention of the head of the Bank of Latvia, was accompanied by a statement from the Latvian Prime Minister that there was no apparent threat to the country's financial system, and it occurred early in the window rather than near the flagged day.

Other candidate items are geopolitical or legal but not obviously price-relevant: escalating airstrikes and a blocked UN truce resolution in Eastern Ghouta, indictments and guilty pleas in the US special counsel investigation, and a statement that North Korea is willing to hold denuclearisation talks.
Announced trade policy in the window is liberalising and small in scale: South Korea signing free trade agreements with five Central American countries.
China threatened 25% tariffs on 106 U.S. product categories, explicitly including soybeans and Boeing aircraft.
The Chinese measure was framed as a reaction to a preceding U.S. threat of tariffs worth up to $50 billion, establishing an escalating tit-for-tat sequence.
Trade policy was already an active channel of negotiation during the window, with the U.S. and South Korea reaching agreements on trade and steel tariffs earlier in the period.
A separate U.S. political item on the flag day reported that Mueller had told the President's lawyers he is considered more than a witness but not under criminal investigation.
Earlier in the window the U.S. government avoided a shutdown when a $1.3 trillion omnibus spending bill was signed into law, removing a near-term fiscal risk.

A parallel geopolitical thread ran through the window: reciprocal diplomatic expulsions between Russia and the United States, EU endorsement of UK attribution of a poisoning to Russia, Russian denials and counter-questions, and technical findings that a Novichok agent was used though its source was uncertain.
The Office of the United States Trade Representative published a list of approximately $200 billion of Chinese goods to be covered by its next round of tariffs.
David Davis resigned as the UK's Secretary of State for Exiting the European Union amid disagreements with the Prime Minister over Brexit negotiations.
The U.S. and Russian presidents held a summit in Helsinki during the window, and separately the U.S. government charged a Russian national with conspiracy to act as an unregistered foreign agent.
Iran began work at a facility capable of producing rotors for up to 60 centrifuges per day, and unrest and casualties were reported across Iraqi provinces.
Items on the flagged day concern a domestic sentencing in South Korea, a stabbing on a bus in Germany, and a protest in Tehran, none of which carry evident cross-asset market significance.
A large share of the window's items are natural disasters, sporting results and human-interest stories with no direct financial-market channel.
A British transport minister resigned over the Prime Minister's Brexit plan and called for a second referendum.
The Prime Minister obtained cabinet approval for the Brexit plan, but many Conservative and opposition MPs voiced strong disapproval.
The Brexit Secretary (Dominic Raab) and Work and Pensions Secretary (Esther McVey) resigned and were replaced by Stephen Barclay and Amber Rudd.
Nissan chairman and former CEO Carlos Ghosn, who is also chairman and CEO of Renault, was arrested in Japan for breaching financial trading laws, and Nissan recommended he and a director step down.
The APEC summit ended without a communiqué for the first time in the forum's history.
The European Union reached a provisional agreement on a system to investigate foreign investments into Europe.
A US federal judge ordered a suspension of construction on the Keystone XL pipeline over an inadequate environmental review.

Contested and unresolved US election outcomes persisted through the window, including a mandatory Florida recount with fraud claims made without evidence, and a Georgia candidate declining to concede while announcing a federal lawsuit.
The Pentagon reported it had begun withdrawing U.S. troops from Syria, while stating the campaign against ISIL was not over.
Kurdish-led forces had days earlier seized Hajin, described as the last major ISIL-held town in Syria, providing the stated rationale context for the drawdown.

Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou faced extradition to the United States on charges of conspiracy to defraud financial institutions in order to evade U.S. sanctions on Iran, and was granted bail with restrictions by a Canadian judge during the window.
The U.S. President replaced his White House Chief of Staff, appointing the incumbent budget director as acting chief of staff.
The Trump Foundation agreed to dissolve under judicial supervision amid a New York lawsuit.
On the flag day, London's Gatwick Airport was shut down intermittently because of drone sightings, affecting hundreds of thousands of passengers, in what police called a deliberate act of disruption.
Political instability also appeared in Europe, with the Belgian Prime Minister submitting his cabinet's resignation to the King after his largest coalition partner quit over the migration compact.
Large-scale street protests with mass detentions and injuries occurred in France during the window, and a terrorist attack on a Strasbourg Christmas market killed five people in total.
On the flagged day, a short-term agreement was announced with congressional leaders to reopen the U.S. federal government after a 35-day partial shutdown.
The agreement is a three-week stop-gap containing no funding for the proposed border barrier, leaving the underlying dispute unresolved.

The shutdown had already produced concrete disruption during the window, with roughly 42,000 active-duty Coast Guard members missing a scheduled paycheck, described as the first such non-payment of U.S. servicemembers during a lapse in appropriations.

The shutdown had also escalated into an institutional standoff, with the President postponing the House Speaker's foreign trip and the Speaker declining to authorise the State of the Union in the House chamber until the shutdown ended.

Two days before the flag, an opposition leader swore himself in as President of Venezuela and was recognised by the United States, Canada and several Latin American nations, while the incumbent refused to recognise the claim.

The Venezuelan situation had been deteriorating through the window, with the opposition leader briefly detained, a National Guard mutiny quashed, and deaths during protests in Caracas and Estado Bolivar.

Earlier in the window, the UK government's Brexit deal was defeated in Parliament by 432 to 202, described as the worst defeat for a Prime Minister in modern British history, though the government then survived a no-confidence vote by 19.
Brexit uncertainty persisted later in the window, with an opposition amendment proposed requiring a second referendum before exit.
At least 46 members of India's security forces were killed by a suicide bomber striking a military convoy in Jammu and Kashmir.
On the day the model flagged, Spain's Prime Minister called a snap general election and announced the dissolution of the Cortes Generales after failing to approve a government budget.
Political conflict in Spain had already escalated earlier in the window, with the central government breaking off dialogue with the Catalan government.
Russia suspended participation in the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty and said it would develop new missiles in response to the U.S. withdrawal.

Venezuela's crisis intensified during the window: aid deliveries were physically blocked at the Colombian border, the interim president did not rule out seeking U.S. military help, and authorities alleged a U.S.-owned freight company delivered weapons.
A suicide bombing in southeastern Iran killed at least 27 Iranian Revolutionary Guards.
Preparations for a second U.S.",
A second U.S.-North Korea summit was announced during the State of the Union and North Korean officials arrived in Beijing ahead of it on the final day of the window.
The only explicitly business-and-economy items in the window are two corporate bankruptcies of limited scale: a German airline ceasing operations and a private Dutch Mars-colonisation organisation.
The UK Prime Minister formally wrote to the European Council President requesting a delay to Brexit.
Approximately one million people marched in London demanding a further referendum on Brexit.
The Prime Minister announced she would resign before the next phase of negotiations if her deal passed, although no vote on that deal was scheduled at the time.
Parliament held indicative votes on eight Brexit options and none secured a majority, with a further round planned for the following Monday.
A Special Counsel report on election interference was delivered to the Attorney General, who days later released a four-page letter of principal conclusions to Congress.
A rocket attack in Israel injured seven people and was followed by Israeli air strikes on multiple Gaza targets, prompting the Israeli Prime Minister to cut short a US trip.
On the flagged day, an Icelandic low-cost airline ceased operations and Venezuela's opposition leader was barred from public office for 15 years.

Other corporate and regulatory events in the window included a $71.3 billion media acquisition completing, a €1.49 billion EU antitrust fine on a large technology firm, a $1.3 billion asset-management software acquisition, a securities regulator alleging massive fraud by a major automaker, and a $775 million pharmaceutical litigation settlement.
On the final day of the window, the United States demanded that all countries cease purchasing oil from Iran by a set date or face sanctions, explicitly aimed at cutting Iran's income.

The days immediately preceding the flag contained a cluster of violent security events, including a foiled armed attack in Riyadh and a coordinated suicide and gun attack on a government ministry in Kabul.
A wave of attacks in Sri Lanka prompted the government to block access to all social media platforms the day before the flag.

Earlier in the window, a Libyan armed force stated it would continue its advance on Tripoli despite international calls to halt, and its commander met the Egyptian president who had backed the operation.
The window also contained macro signals of weakening trade, with Singapore reporting its largest year-on-year monthly drop in non-oil exports since a prior reference period, led by electronics.

Political and policy events during the window included a UK-EU agreement to delay Brexit, the release of a redacted special counsel report in the United States, and an opposition candidate winning Ukraine's presidential run-off with over 70 percent.
Google withdrew Android update support, the Google Play Store and Gmail from Huawei phones after the company was blacklisted by the US Commerce Department.
The US administration announced a second aid package worth $16 billion for farmers affected by trade measures.
The United States lifted tariffs on steel and aluminium from Canada and Mexico early in the window, indicating active and shifting trade policy.
The UK Prime Minister announced her resignation as Conservative Party leader, remaining in office only until a successor is elected.
British Steel Limited entered compulsory liquidation after rescue talks between the government and its owners failed, affecting around 5,000 workers.
The US ordered 1,500 troops and several Patriot missile launchers to the Persian Gulf as tensions with Iran rose.
Rhetorical escalation between the US and Iran preceded the deployment, with Iran's foreign minister responding to US statements about 'the official end of Iran'.
European Parliament elections were held across multiple member states during the window, alongside Belgian federal elections.
Italy's Deputy Prime Minister filed a vote of no-confidence against the Prime Minister early in the window.
On the flag day, the President of Italy accepted the Prime Minister's resignation, formally ending the government.
Argentina's peso fell to record lows after the incumbent President's loss in a primary vote, and the Treasury Minister resigned as a result.
The US Trade Representative announced a delay for a significant number of products subject to a previously announced 10% import tariff.
Hong Kong International Airport was effectively locked down when all departing flights were cancelled amid unrest, and later protests drew claims of 1.7 million participants.
The US President stated publicly that intelligence indicated China was moving troops toward the Hong Kong border.
A ransomware attack hit the computer systems of 23 towns in Texas, attributed to a single threat actor.

The items dated to the flag day itself concern a Paris transport strike affecting two of sixteen metro lines, U.S. Treasury cyber-related sanctions on a North Korean-linked hacking group, and a celebrity sentencing in a college admissions case — none of which has evident scale for broad market pricing.
The day before the flag contained only a French parliamentary corruption investigation, Twitter account suspensions of Cuban officials, and a rail disaster in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The clearest macro-relevant item in the window is an early-window report that U.S. manufacturing activity contracted for the first time in three years, but it falls ten days before the flagged day.
Argentina reinstated currency controls by emergency decree early in the window, a country-specific financial event also well before the flagged day.

Several items describe the partial defusing of previously live political risks: legislation passed to block a no-deal exit from the European Union, the formal withdrawal of the Hong Kong extradition bill, and the swearing-in of a new Italian coalition cabinet.

Ongoing UK political instability continued through the window, including loss of the government's working majority, rejection of an early election motion, a court ruling that the parliamentary suspension was unlawful, and publication of no-deal contingency plans.
Turkey's president publicly threatened to invade SDF-held areas of northern Syria "today or tomorrow" and dismissed the joint US-Turkish buffer-zone patrols as a "fairy tale".
On the final day of the window, both the SDF and Turkey said the United States had begun withdrawing troops from Syrian areas near the Turkish border.

A prominent US senator described the withdrawal as "a big win for Iran and Assad [and] a big win for ISIL", and a former US envoy warned that 60,000 SDF-held ISIL detainees could form the "nucleus for a resurgent ISIL".
The US Department of Defense expelled Turkey from the Combined Air Operations Centre, cutting its access to surveillance information on SDF positions.

A formal impeachment inquiry into the US president was announced at the start of the window, followed by the resignation of the US special envoy to Ukraine a day after a whistleblower report on a call with Ukraine's president, an "urgent" State Department inspector general briefing to congressional staff, and the president's personal lawyer retaining counsel.

Other regional stress present in the window includes Houthi claims of a major cross-border attack near Najran, Turkey stating it cannot stop buying Iranian oil despite US sanctions, and Syria demanding withdrawal of US and Turkish forces.

Escalating civil unrest with heavy casualties and an internet blackout occurred in Iraq, and Ecuador declared a state of emergency over fuel-price protests that blocked the capital's transport network.

Corporate distress in consumer-facing sectors appeared repeatedly: a Chapter 11 filing with up to 178 store closures, another retailer closing 60 stores on declining profits, and government responses in two countries to a travel company's collapse.
North Korea tested a new submarine-launched ballistic missile while also saying it would resume working-level nuclear talks with the United States.

The US FCC unanimously designated Huawei and ZTE as national security risks, barred them from the Universal Service Fund, and ordered national wireless carriers to remove their equipment from existing networks.
China's Foreign Minister publicly accused the United States at the G20 meeting of being the "world's biggest destabilizing factor" and of "smearing China everywhere".

The US President signed the Hong Kong Human Rights and Democracy Act into law despite strong Chinese opposition; the law conditions US trade with Hong Kong on the territory retaining sufficient autonomy and bans export of crowd-control munitions to its police.
Iraqi protesters stormed and set fire to the Iranian Consulate General in Najaf.
Iraqi security forces killed dozens of protesters in Nasiriyah, Najaf and Baghdad in one of the deadliest days of the protest movement, and violence continued the following day.
The Prime Minister of Iraq announced plans to offer his resignation to parliament in reaction to the protest movement.

Saudi Arabia's King blamed Iran for missile and drone attacks and said his country would not hesitate to defend itself, while the head of Iran's Revolutionary Guards delivered a televised "we will destroy you" threat aimed at Israel, Saudi Arabia and the United States.

Items dated on the flagged day itself concern a domestic vaccination travel restriction, a factory explosion in Khartoum, and the resignation of Finland's Prime Minister over handling of industrial strikes.
A rocket attack on K-1 Air Base in Kirkuk killed an American civilian contractor and injured US and Iraqi troops.

The US conducted unilateral airstrikes inside Iraq against Kata'ib Hezbollah, which the Iraqi Prime Minister condemned as a violation of sovereignty and a dangerous escalation, and which Iran called illegal.
Supporters stormed the US embassy in Baghdad in response to the airstrikes; they withdrew the following day on orders from the Popular Mobilization Forces.
Quds Force commander Qasem Soleimani was killed in a US airstrike in Baghdad, alongside Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis and others; strikes were carried out against two targets linked to Iran in Baghdad.
Senior Iranian figures publicly promised "vigorous revenge against America" and state television replaced broadcasts with prayers; Esmail Ghaani was appointed to replace Soleimani.
The United States deployed over 3,000 additional soldiers to the Middle East as tensions with Iran heightened.
Iran's parliament voted to exit the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action nuclear deal.
Militants fired rockets at Iraqi bases supporting US personnel, nearly hitting the US Embassy in Baghdad, and the US-led coalition paused anti-ISIL operations to protect its troops.

On the final day, Iran's legislature formally designated the US Department of Defense a terrorist organisation, and Germany announced a partial withdrawal of its troops from Iraq citing security concerns.
Protests over the killing spread beyond Iraq and Iran, including demonstrations in Karachi, Pakistan.
The World Health Organization officially declared the outbreak a pandemic during the window.
Stock and bond markets fell together for the first time since the prior financial crisis, described as a massive portfolio sell-off with investors seeking cash.

The Federal Reserve made an emergency full-percentage-point rate cut, announced a $700 billion quantitative easing programme, set reserve requirements to zero and lowered other lending rates — its largest single-day set of measures — less than two weeks after a previous unscheduled intervention.
On the flagged day, the U.S. Senate voted down a stimulus relief package for the second time.

Governments imposed sweeping economic shutdowns: Pennsylvania ordered all non-life-sustaining businesses closed, West Virginia closed restaurant dining rooms, bars and casinos, and Argentina imposed a mandatory national quarantine.
Corporate distress and state intervention appeared: Apple closed all stores outside China, Laura Ashley collapsed into administration, and Italy announced it would take over flag carrier Alitalia.

Fiscal and administrative emergency measures were taken, including a UK wage-subsidy stimulus plan, U.S. suspension of foreclosures and evictions plus invocation of the Defense Production Act, and postponement of U.S. Tax Day.

Case and death counts accelerated sharply in Italy, Spain and elsewhere, with Italy's toll rising from 827 to 2,978 within the window and Spain recording its largest single-day death total with the Prime Minister saying "the worst is yet to come".
Cross-border travel was widely suspended, including Germany closing borders with five neighbours, the U.S. and Canada suspending nonessential travel, and India suspending international flight entry.
The final day of the window contains a single, contentless placeholder item about the pandemic in Asia, with no described event.

The penultimate day's items concern localised violence, an election round, a doctor's death, a national record daily death toll in Russia, and a U.S. state lawsuit against China — none of which are of evident scale for global asset pricing.

The only explicitly economic items in the window are a €540 billion EU loan package agreed by finance ministers, a regulatory approval for a foreign bank to take majority control of a Chinese securities firm, a Korean bank's $86 million settlement, and one carmaker resuming production — all early or mid-window and modest in scope.

The dominant content of the window is a continuing public health emergency: record single-day death tolls in several countries, lockdown extensions, and case-count milestones, which are a persistent backdrop rather than a discrete late-window shock.

Policy direction in the latter half of the window was mixed but tilted toward reopening rather than fresh restriction, with shops reopening in Germany alongside a warning about a second wave, and antibody testing announced ahead of a planned economic reopening in New York.

Geopolitical items late in the window include increased Iranian naval patrols in the Persian Gulf after a naval confrontation, but no accompanying commercial, shipping, or commodity consequence is described.
Winter Storm Uri was reported to have killed at least 23 people and caused power outages for millions of people across the United States two days before the flag date.
The US Senate passed a budget resolution 51–50, with the Vice President casting the tiebreaking vote, as a step toward passing a $1.9 trillion stimulus package without Republican support.
The White House announced an extension of the foreclosure ban and mortgage forbearance to address the pandemic's economic impact.
The IAEA confirmed Iran had produced uranium metal at Isfahan, described as a major breach of the nuclear deal.
Houthi forces carried out a drone strike on Abha International Airport in Saudi Arabia, damaging a civilian aircraft.
Japan reported a 4.8% annual GDP contraction, its first annual contraction in years, attributed to the pandemic.

Several jurisdictions reimposed or extended restrictions during the window, including a five-day Stage 4 lockdown in Victoria with all international flights to Melbourne cancelled, a stay-at-home order for two million people in Vietnam's Hai Duong province, and extended lockdowns in Greece.

Counterweighting the restriction news, large vaccine supply and procurement announcements accumulated, including a US deal for 200 million Moderna and Pfizer doses and an EU deal for an additional 300 million Moderna doses.
A limited clinical trial suggested the Oxford–AstraZeneca vaccine was weak against the 501.V2 variant, while the WHO subsequently recommended the vaccine for all adults worldwide.

A ransomware cyberattack shut in the largest US fuel pipeline, which moves 2.5 million barrels a day and supplies 45 percent of the East Coast's diesel, gasoline and jet fuel, and the US president declared a state of emergency in response.
The World Health Organization classified the B.1.617 lineage as a "Variant of Concern", the fourth such designation.
India reported successive global records for daily cases and deaths through the window, exceeding 400,000 daily cases and 4,187 daily deaths, and surpassed 20 million cumulative cases.

Multiple governments imposed travel restrictions tied to the variant, including US restrictions on travel from India, Australian flight suspensions, and UK red-listing of Turkey, the Maldives and Nepal.
The variant was detected in a rapidly widening set of countries during the window, including Portugal, Romania, Jordan, Malaysia, Mexico, Algeria, Morocco, Kenya and South Africa.
Clashes between Palestinian protesters and Israeli police in East Jerusalem's Old City injured at least 90 Palestinians on Day 12.
A US Coast Guard cutter fired 30 warning shots at 13 Iranian fast-attack craft harassing US Navy warships in the Strait of Hormuz on Day 14.

Offsetting positive news included US and Canadian authorisation of the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine for ages 12-15, a large new EU vaccine purchase agreement, and reopening steps in France, Spain, Denmark and Florida.

The window is dominated by routine pandemic reporting: record daily case counts across many countries driven by the Omicron variant, with no accompanying reports of new broad economic shutdowns in major economies.
Several governments responded to the case surge by loosening rather than tightening restrictions, shortening isolation periods to protect staffing and economic activity.

There is unrest in Kazakhstan involving deaths, a shoot-to-kill order and a request for foreign military assistance, but the items contain no reference to commodity supply, energy output or financial market effects.

Two China-related corporate/regulatory items appear — Evergrande suspending trading in its shares ahead of a restructuring, and new cybersecurity review requirements for large Chinese companies seeking foreign listings — but neither item describes a wider market reaction.
Geopolitical items on the final days are limited to announced Russia-Belarus war games and an arrest of an alleged Russian intelligence agent in Ukraine, with no escalation described.

The items dated on the flag day itself concern a national death milestone, the death of the European Parliament president, an isolation-period change and a national case record — none of which carries evident market significance.
Gazprom announced it would stop delivering natural gas to Poland via the Yamal–Europe pipeline and to Bulgaria after both rejected demands to pay in roubles.
The following day Gazprom stated supplies to PGNiG and Bulgargaz were 'completely suspended', and Poland, Bulgaria and the EU condemned the move.
Bulgaria is described as almost completely dependent on Russian gas, so the suspension poses a serious challenge to its security of supply, while Poland does not expect disruption.
An item in the window is labelled as a Russia–European Union gas dispute.
Russia's foreign minister said weapons supplied to Ukraine would be legitimate targets and that NATO is engaged in a proxy war, saying 'War means war.'
Germany announced delivery of 50 Gepard anti-air tanks, its first heavy weaponry supplied since the start of the invasion.
The UK Foreign Secretary said Russian forces must be pushed out of the whole of Ukraine including territory captured eight years earlier.
Attacks were reported on the Transnistrian state security ministry building, and drones were later reported near the Cobasna ammunition depot, indicating possible spillover beyond Ukraine.
Earlier in the window a Russian general said the operation's goal now included a land corridor from Crimea toward Transnistria.
Russian strikes hit energy and transport infrastructure including the Kremenchuk oil refinery, rail stations and a strategic bridge in Odessa Oblast.
Earlier in the window a ratings agency signalled it would declare Russia in default at the end of a grace period if dollar bonds were serviced in roubles.
Shanghai reported record case counts and then tightened lockdown enforcement as cases continued to rise.
Peru declared a state of emergency at the Las Bambas copper mine, suspending rights of assembly and protest.
Russian forces announced a retreat from Kherson city and the west bank of the Dnieper.
Ukrainian troops entered Kherson, ending an eight-month occupation of the only regional capital Russia had captured.
The Bank of England raised rates by 0.75 percentage points to 3.00%, its largest increase in 33 years, and forecast a record-length recession.

UK cost-of-living pressure intensified, with record grocery inflation of 14.7% and 27% of households reporting financial struggle, and the Royal College of Nursing announcing its first strike in 106 years.
Turkish inflation reached 85.51% amid an ongoing currency and debt crisis.
US election results reported during the window included a Massachusetts governor's race and the Nevada Senate race that secured a Democratic Senate majority.
Putin was confirmed as not attending the G20 summit in Bali in person.
The US announced a further $400 million weapons package for Ukraine, and said North Korea was secretly supplying artillery shells to Russia.
Day 14 items concern EU sanctions on Iranian entities, a UK-France Channel migration agreement and detentions after a bombing in Turkey, none of which are of obvious broad market significance.
A magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck Gaziantep Province, Turkey, on Day 11, with at least 3,400 people reported killed across Turkey and Syria.
A second earthquake of magnitude 7.5 struck Kahramanmaraş, Turkey, nine hours after the first.

The disaster was still generating disorder at the end of the window: three inmates were killed and twelve injured when soldiers opened fire during a prison riot in Hatay Province, Turkey, by prisoners demanding to see families affected by the earthquake.

Two days before the earthquake, the US Federal Aviation Administration closed airspace off the east coast and suspended arrivals at three airports after the president ordered a high-altitude balloon shot down over the Atlantic.

Separate items in the window point to macroeconomic strain: PayPal announced roughly 2,000 job cuts citing a challenging macro-economic environment, Flybe collapsed into administration, and Lebanon's central bank devalued its currency by 90%.
More than 500,000 UK public sector workers struck in the largest industrial action there in decades, and France was experiencing pension reform strikes.
Rebel forces led by Tahrir al-Sham advanced from Idlib into Aleppo, then Hama, Salamiyah and Homs over the course of the window.
Rebel forces seized the Presidential Palace in Damascus and Sednaya Prison, releasing thousands of prisoners.
Russian state media reported that Bashar al-Assad and his family were in Moscow and had been granted asylum, following speculation about a plane that disappeared from radar near Homs.
A Syrian opposition figure, Mohammed al-Bashir, was appointed prime minister of a transitional government on the final day of the window.
Israel launched airstrikes on Syrian air bases and on a research centre overseeing chemical weapons and ballistic missile programmes.
Iran evacuated military personnel, diplomatic staff and civilians from Syria, and Jordan closed its border after rebels seized the main crossing.
The UN estimated the renewed Syrian conflict could displace around 1.5 million people, and the UN envoy called for an orderly political transition.
South Korea's president declared martial law, protesters attempted to storm the National Assembly, impeachment proceedings began, and he subsequently apologised.
The French government fell after 331 of 577 deputies backed a no-confidence motion.
Romania's Constitutional Court annulled the first round of the presidential election two days before the runoff.
A separate front opened between Turkish-backed forces and Kurdish SDF units, with fighting in Manbij producing 50 deaths on the final day.
A ceasefire in Lebanon was agreed at the start of the window but was followed by mutual accusations of violation and continued exchanges of fire.
Indian airstrikes hit multiple locations in Pakistan and Pakistan-administered Kashmir, killing at least eight people.
Pakistan launched retaliatory strikes into India and Indian-administered Kashmir and claimed to have destroyed five Indian fighter jets, with three civilians killed.
Pakistan's prime minister declared the Indian attacks an act of war and vowed further retaliation.
Border skirmishes between India and Pakistan were already being reported earlier in the window.
Pakistan's information minister publicly warned several days earlier that India intended to strike within 24 to 36 hours.

Separately, US trade policy actions continued, with the administration terminating the de minimis tariff exemption for some consumer imports, prompting price changes at Shein and Temu and a shipping pause by Temu.
Germany cut its growth forecast to zero, with its central bank estimating a future recession, and the economics minister attributed the crisis primarily to US tariffs.

A ballistic missile from Houthi-controlled Yemen struck near Ben Gurion International Airport, followed by Israeli strikes on Hudaydah Port and then a US–Houthi ceasefire brokered by Oman under which the Houthis agreed to stop disrupting international shipping.
Berkshire Hathaway's CEO announced he would step down by year-end, with a named successor pending board approval.
A widespread power outage affected Spain, Portugal, Andorra and parts of France, shutting airports, transit and hospitals, with fatalities reported the following day.
Thai F-16 jets struck Cambodian military targets in Oddar Meanchey and Preah Vihear, killing four Cambodian civilians and wounding ten.
Cambodian shelling of Ubon Ratchathani province killed a Thai soldier and injured eight others.
The conflict spilled into civil life, with heightened security for Cambodian athletes at the SEA Games in Bangkok and Cambodia subsequently withdrawing its entire delegation on security grounds.
The US Coast Guard seized an oil tanker off Venezuela that was en route to Cuba and flying a Guyanese flag without being registered there.
A US Navy strike destroyed a boat in the Pacific alleged to be carrying narcotics, killing four.
Netflix agreed to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery for US$72 billion, described as one of the largest entertainment-industry takeovers.
Airbus issued an emergency software update affecting 6,000 A320 aircraft worldwide, causing major travel disruption.
On the flag day, the Zhelyazkov Government resigned after weeks of mass protests over economic policy and alleged corruption.
Also on the flag day, the Greek finance minister was elected president of the Eurogroup.
Russia said its forces captured Pokrovsk in Donetsk Oblast, and the UK sanctioned Russia's GRU over the Novichok attack findings.

Oil prices moved sharply on Middle East de-escalation expectations, with WTI falling 6.2% to $92.94 and Brent 3.77% to $95.61 in a single session, and UK stocks rising on hopes of new Iran–U.S. talks.
A closure/blockade of the Strait of Hormuz was central to the crisis, with Iran threatening to close the strait again if a blockade is not lifted and a tanker reportedly attacked by Iranian gunboats.
The disruption produced measurable real-economy effects: rolling power cuts in Pakistan, a record Norwegian crude export value, and Lufthansa cutting 20,000 short-haul flights on fuel costs.
Physical transit through the strait resumed during the window, with the first cruise ship crossing since the start of the war and a South Korean tanker using an alternative Red Sea route.

Escalation risk remained live mid-window: the U.S. defense secretary said combat operations could resume absent a permanent deal, Trump said he was 'highly unlikely' to renew the ceasefire, and Israel's defence minister said the country was prepared to resume military action.
In the last third of the window the ceasefire was extended by three weeks and a second round of Iran–U.S. talks in Islamabad was confirmed with named U.S. envoys.

Equity markets reached records shortly after the ceasefire extension, with the Nikkei 225 above 60,000 for the first time and the KOSPI at a record high, while Asia-Pacific markets opened mixed on lingering geopolitical uncertainty.

Supply damage was described as persistent: a major trading house estimated at least one billion barrels of lost production, and the IEA estimated 120 billion cubic metres of lost LNG supply and a strained gas market for at least two years.

Military and shipping risk in the region remained on the agenda late in the window, with Germany announcing naval units including a minesweeper for a potential Strait of Hormuz mission, and pirates hijacking a cargo ship off Puntland on the final day.
A ceasefire/peace agreement between Iran and the United States was announced mid-window, including a 60-day extension and reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, with signing planned in Switzerland.
Oil prices fell about 5% on the announcement that the war would end, the strait would reopen and the US blockade would end, demonstrating direct market sensitivity to this news thread.
US equity indices had earlier risen when a round of strikes against Iran was cancelled, confirming the same headline sensitivity in equities.

Iran asserted that the Strait of Hormuz would be under Iranian and Omani sovereignty and subject to a fee, and later announced it would begin charging transit fees at the end of the 60-day agreement period.

Claims about the strait's status were directly contradictory: US Central Command said 55 ships carrying over 17 million barrels had crossed and traffic had increased, rejecting Iranian claims the waterway was closed.

Observed transits collapsed to five known ships from 26 the previous day, described as occurring amid the closure, with only two crude tankers carrying 2 million barrels reported transiting the following day.
The final day of the window carries an item headed as a Strait of Hormuz crisis.
The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve was reported at its lowest level in years after drawing 9 million barrels per week during the war, reducing the buffer against a supply disruption.
A fuel crisis associated with the war was recorded during the window.
QatarEnergy's plan to resume LNG production was contingent on the strait officially reopening, linking gas supply to the same chokepoint.

The ceasefire framework was described by Iran's foreign ministry as practically meaningless, and Iran/Hezbollah alleged repeated Israeli violations, while Israel ruled out withdrawal from southern Lebanon and Israeli soldiers were killed in a firefight with Hezbollah.
On the flagged day the US Senate voted 50–48 to require the administration to halt military action against Iran, joining the House.
